subsubtopic: PETITION RESPECTING FUTURE OF PETROCHEMICAL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to remind the House of the fact that I recently tabled in the House of Commons a petition containing 11,000 names, which petition is an indication of the concern of people for the future of the petrochemical industry.
True to the generosity of spirit of the people who signed such petition, they were not seeking short and long-term assistance for the oil based petrochemical industry alone, but for the petrochemical industry as a whole. These people are also realistic enough to appreciate that a Government decision based on the task force report will take some time because there is not unanimity of approach, and any such decision must take into account the views expressed by the oil based and gas based petrochemical industries, plus the concerns of Quebec, Ontario, and Alberta, and the fact that inappropriate action could lead to countervailing measures from the United States.
The people concerned and the people employed in this industry, however, have a right to expect an early decision, and hopefully one that provides for short-term and long-term
assistance.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR RECOGNITION OF HONORARY CONSULS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, prior to the changing of the Standing Orders there was a Motion under Standing Order 43 last year which was joined in by the Member for London West (Mr. Burghardt), and the Hon. Member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky), which read in these terms:
That this House, in recognition of the contribution to Canada of Canadians of Latvian, Lithuanian and Estonian descent, welcome their honorary consul and representatives of the respective communities to the Tenth Annual Baltic Evening on Parliament Hill.
That motion was accepted unanimously at that time by the House. It is no longer possible for us to move such a Motion, but it is appropriate that, on the occasion of the Eleventh Annual Baltic Evening on Parliament Hill, all Members of Parliament commemorate the contribution to Canada of Canadians of Latvian, Lithuanian, and Estonian descent, and on their behalf 1 make this request.
For many years it has been the wish of countless Canadians that the Honorary Consuls of Estonia and Latvia join the Honorary Consul of Lithuania and be recognized in the diplomatic corps publications of the Government of Canada. I know that this request is supported by Members of all Parties in this House as a simple yet profound method of honouring those Canadians who walk among us as living reminders of the importance of our rights and freedoms as Canadians.

Since this piece of legislation was introduced into the House over a year ago, the support for Canagrex has become more and more evident. Recently, in convention, the 200,000 strong membership of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture once again expressed their support for an agricultural products export agency and its immediate need. The farmers of this country feel, as I do, that agriculture is the industry which can help put our economy back on its feet. The time has come to give the people of Canada an export mechanism to do just that and give this nation an opportunity to expand its agri-food international trade market.
This piece of legislation has been before the House for almost 14 months now. It has spent four months before the Standing Committee on Agriculture where it received 14 amendments. Bill C-85 has been talked about enough; it is now time to act. The farmers of the country look forward to its immediate passage.

Madam Speaker, yesterday the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) belittled remarks by the Elon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) which accurately outlined the consequences of the Government's embrace of socialism. He said:
We on this side of the House believe in social justice within a free enterprise system.
What a joke! He had not been paying attention to the philosophy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who stated:
We have not been able to make it work, the free enterprise system ... that means the Government is going to take a larger role in running institutions.
And it has been. When asked by a group of students what type of society he would choose-socialist or capitalist, this was the Prime Minister's reply:
Labour Party socialism, or Cuban socialism, or Chinese socialism-
Socialism is nothing more than state control, something abhorrent to Canadians, and we are getting it in spades-state withholding of property rights; state control of communications; state control of energy; state control of culture, state control of agriculture, with closure on the Canagrex Bill, and state destruction of transport and the Armed Forces.
We of the Progressive Conservative Party are the only opposition to this type of control by the state.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council may naively believe that all this, coupled with repressive taxation, the proliferation of non-audited Crown Corporations, arbitrary metric and bilingualism, equates with his espousal yesterday of "social justice within a free enterprise system". It is not ours. Loss of economic freedom means loss of individual freedom. His constituents and other Canadians recognize the Government's slippery slide to socialism. He obviously does not.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVISION OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this day is of special significance to the Canadian Lithuanian Community as they are remembering the founding of Lithuania on February 16, 1918. The first recorded Lithuanian immigrants to Canada arrived at the beginning of the nineteenth century. Lithuanians will be pleased to see that the second edition of the Languages of the World map has been revised to include language groups such as the Lithuanians. This is to the credit of several multicultural groups who drew this matter to the attention of the Commissioner of Official Languages.
With the official recognition of Canada's multicultural heritage in Section 27 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, it is now time to revise Section 38 of the Official Languages Act. This Section, which refers to language groups other than English or French in a negative fashion, should be rewritten in the positive style found in Section 27 of the Charter.
The role of the Commissioner of Official Languages should be expanded to include the area of multicuituralism, with the Commissioner becoming the Commissioner of Official Languages and Multicuituralism. Furthermore, a conference on bilingualism and multicuituralism should be convened in the near future to re-examine these areas of national significance, and I know that Dauphin would be delighted to host such a conference.

To the Government of Canada, multicuituralism is the expression of differing views, traditions and backgrounds of Canadians. It is important to recognize the great contribution that various ethnocultural groups have made to Canada. Many of these people, while able to express their views and traditions freely in this country, are unable to do so in their own homelands. I am speaking today specifically with regard to the Baltic nations, and the Estonians, Latvians, and Lithuanians, a group who have attempted to preserve their culture and heritage in Canada while unable to do so in their countries of origin.
Canada does not recognize de jure the forcible occupation of the Baltic states. It is fitting on the day of the Baltic Evening, and on the day of the sixty-fifth anniversary of the Declaration of the Independence of Lithuania, to remember the contribution that these people have made to Canada.

subsubtopic: FIRING OF ASSISTANT DEPUTY MINISTER OF LABOUR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not going to congratulate anyone. This is going to be strictly according to the rules. Last week, a Montreal newspaper reported a million-dollar mistake for which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) must take the responsibility. It all started when Assistant Deputy Minister Andre Deom, who was hired by the Department of Labour in January 1981, was fired in May 1982. After a dispute with the Deputy Minister, the Government made a private arrangement with Mr. Deom, who since the first of October last year has been receiving $6,700 per month tax free, and will do so for a period of two years, which adds up to a grand total of $160,800 or $280,000 before taxes. speechtext:

On previous occasions in the House I have asked the Minister whether she would be prepared to table any drafts of the Act which might be in existence. She should also be prepared to refer the whole matter to the Health and Welfare Committee. Canadians who are concerned about the Canada Health Act and want to have an opinion on it before it actually comes to the House could then have a chance to express their views and, no doubt, lend support to any intention of the Government to eliminate extra billing and other ways in which user pay mechanisms are eating away at the principles of medicare.

moral edge in the medicare debate and have leverage over Progressive Conservative provincial Governments that are hostile to the principles of medicare. Member for Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker) is still in his seat and I am now in a position to rule on the point of order he raised last Friday concerning the fact that a document tabled the Thursday, February 10, 1983 by the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) was not deemed referred to a Committee of the House.
Standing Order 46(1) stipulates that returns, reports or other papers can be laid before the House in accordance with an Act of Parliament or in pursuance of any resolution or Standing Order of this House.
In addition, Standing Order 46(2) provides that a Minister may table any report or other paper dealing with a matter coming within the administrative responsibilities of the Government. As stated in Citation 379(2) of Beauchesne, these papers may be laid before the House voluntarily.
Let me now quote Standing Order 46(4) as follows:
Reports, returns or other papers laid before the House in accordance with an Act of Parliament shall thereupon be deemed to have been permanently referred to the Committee designated by the Member tabling the report, return or paper.
During the debate on this point of order I indicated how I would read that paragraph but I decided to read it again privately and meditate on it. The key words are "in accordance with an Act of Parliament".
In the case before us, the tabling of the document was not required by an Act of Parliament, but it was tabled on the initiative of the Minister as provided in Standing Order 46(2). I must rule that the document in question does not come under the purview of Standing Order 46(4) and, therefore, there is no point of order.

speechtext:
that Bill C-583, an Act to amend the Canada Elections Act (deposit), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Madam Speaker, Bill C-583 has been in my mind and in the minds of a number of people who have assisted me in elections for some considerable period of time. The Bill involves the matter of the deposit that a candidate in an election must place with the returning officer in the riding in order to be a candidate.
The deposit under Section 23(2)(j) of the Canada Elections Act has been the princely sum of $200 since 1882. The purpose of my Bill is to increase that figure of 1882 to a more realistic figure in light of today's economic conditions namely to the sum of $2,000.
Over a hundred years ago a deposit of $200 was a great deal of money. Indeed, a lot of people who worked a whole year did not earn $200. It was a very significant sum. It was real honest money that people put up in order to be a candidate in an election. Until very recently, unless a candidate got half the winner's vote he lost or forfeited his deposit. The concept of the deposit was to ensure that those who honestly wanted to run for the House of Commons were prepared to put up some
earnest money and to compensate the Crown for the cost of the election. If they did not get a realistic number of votes, they would lose that money.
The sum of $200 has now become a pretty nominal sum. The average industrial wage today is in the area of $385 per week. Therefore, $200 represents just slightly more than half a week's wages for the average industrial wager earner. It is not really earnest deposit money; it is nothing but a shell in the total organization of an election.
For very little money, someone can be a candidate in a federal election. Some do this for personal reasons, wanting to have their name before the public, advertising their name, if you like. For $200 you can have your name spread before the City of Mississauga for 60 days or more. The Government will print your name on ballots for some 80,000 electors. You will be publicized in the newspapers. This is all at the expense of the Government of Canada. What a wonderful way to get your name across to the public if you have some kook idea!
You can force your way into every all-candidates meeting in the constituency. I have had that experience. People run honest, all-candidates meetings in my constituency. They try to ensure that the point of view of those seriously running for election is made known to those constituents who are interested. Time and again we have candidates who really have no interest and no possibility of winning. They make no personal effort to win other than to appear at the meeting to make a speech, using up the time of the meeting. Because of this the rest of the community cannot get at the issues they want to discuss.
The $200 deposit has made it possible for people to make a joke of our election system. For a very nominal sum, you are entitled to expenses that, according to the Chief Electoral Officer, cost the Government of Canada an additional $1,000 for every candidate beyond three who runs for election. In other words, if a ballot contains three names, it would cost on average $1,000 to put on an additional name. For $200 a person puts the Government to the expense of $1,000. For that $200 the candidate is entitled to ten copies of the voters' list to do with as he or she wants. You receive the names and addresses, the detail of where every single person who has the right to vote in the federal election lives within a constituency. Not only that, you are entitled to demand from the returning officer an election key and election map. What a wonderful amount of material! The material itself, on a straight paper basis, is worth more than $200.
It really is not a question of being unfair when I ask to raise the deposit level. It is really a question of saying to those who honestly want to run in an election: "Pay your own costs". Is it going to deprive anyone who has a chance of winning? I say it is not.
Under the present Canada Elections Act, if a person receives 15 per cent of the vote or better, that $200 is now returned. Indeed, not only is the $200 returned, but, as we know, under the Elections Expenses Act, virtually all the

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASE IN CANDIDATES' DEPOSIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Election law is one of my hobbies and I have spent the last ten years serving on the Chief Electoral Officer's ad hoc committee on election law, particularly focusing on the elections expenses legislation as well as the Canada Elections Act itself. We have tried to deal with part of the dilemma which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has put forward. That is, how can we provide through the taxpayer a significant amount of money and resources to candidates in an election campaign, and make sure the taxpayer receives a proper and just return on the expenditures he makes on behalf of the election campaign itself? We have been dealing, not on the basis of the $200 deposit, but rather looking at it from the point of view of the resources which are turned over to candidates who may or may not be legitimately in front of the Canadian electorate.
Our dilemma is that it is very difficult to tell who is a legitimate candidate before the electorate at a given point in time. Although you and 1 may have our opinion, Mr. Speaker, I believe we have to recognize that the Social Credit Party, which was represented in this House for a significant number of years, the New Democratic Party, the progressive party which preceded it, the election from time to time of Independents, are all people who have come here legitimately through the electoral system. Any kind of a system which we put in place, it seems to me, should not be designed to cut off legitimate dissent from a Party which may at the particular time hold a majority of the seats in the House of Commons. Rather, the system should be designed to make sure that the people's representatives get elected to the House of Commons no matter what Party they may belong to and no matter whether they choose to run within the political Party system or outside of it. The dilemma which we have is to try to balance off the
Canada Elections Act
requirements for an open electoral system against the kind of thing which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South quite properly pointed out, particularly in the urban areas, of having maybe ten or 11 candidates running, when the general public may be really interested in only three, four or five.
How do we separate, if you will, the sheep from the goats? How do we make sure the electorate is able to have the choice it wishes? It is true, as the Hon. Member pointed out, that the $200 fee has become an anachronism. It no longer has the effect it was designed to have. It was originally designed to have the effect of weeding out on a financial basis the sheep from the goats. In terms of those of us who are here, by and large that sum, whether it be $200 or $2,000, could be met by our constituency organizations, but it might be a barrier to people having a legitimate point of view to get across.
An election is not only about electing individuals to the House of Commons, or selecting Parties to govern; it is also about issues, ideas, and about the debate of those issues and ideas. We would, I believe, be hard put to disentangle from the complexity and carnival atmosphere, in an election campaign, just where personality, party, issues and local ideas are intermixed, Mr. Speaker, and how the individual elector makes his determination as to whom he will vote for on the basis of that. There is no question, however, that the ability in the olden days to put a financial barrier up to prevent people from running was an important one at a time when political Parties were far less organized than they are now.
As Sir John A. Macdonald used to put it, there was an enormous number of loose fish out there to be netted in order for him to be able to carry on his Government. In those days, the Party system was not as rigid as it is today. It was a much looser form of shifting coalitions. Members had far more independence. They represented regional interests in a much more precise and direct way than they do today. Our system has a different kind of structure. We have Parties now which are much more imbedded in the fabric of our society. We have people who belong to those Parties and are prepared to come into the House of Commons, to accept the Party Whip, more or less, of the Party whose banner they ran under. There is a fair amount of freedom in our system still because Parties run for office without a very clear manifesto or a very clear idea of what it is they want to do, as contrasted, for example, with Great Britain, where there is a very precise manifesto. Therefore, the electoral system we deal with is quite different from the system which developed the $50 and then the $200 limit.
I approach the problem from a different perspective than the Hon. Member for Mississauga South. I tend to look at it from the point of view of protecting the interests of the Canadian taxpayer and the Canadian electorate. Obviously, there has to be at some point a balance between having everyone and his uncle running as candidates and providing a selection of candidates which is wide enough to give the electorate an appropriate choice; and, as well, to make sure that appropriate views on policy options and opinions are properly heard so the electorate can vote effectively. In order

February 16, 1983
Canada Elections Act
to do that it needs to have a selection of Parties, individuals, ideas and ideologies.
When a person is nominated as a candidate from a recognized political Party, which may be a Party which is represented in the Elouse of Commons and it may well be one that is not, that person receives a number of benefits which the taxpayer gives to him. He has a certain status in law. In addition, the taxpayers say they will pay the cost of one mailing to all of his constituents. That is a substantial amount of money. It is also a substantial amount of power.
In addition to that, and perhaps more impressive, all candidates receive tax credit forms. We all know the system. If someone gives to my campaign $100, I give him a tax receipt for $75. There are restrictions on how these may be used but they are difficult to enforce. So there is no question that is a very powerful economic tool in the hands of a candidate.
Secondly, there is the problem of what happens to surplus funds. A fringe candidate may be able to collect more money than he cares to spend. What do you do with the surplus funds? That is also an important question because those are basically taxpayers' funds. They do not belong to the candidate; they are given by the taxpayers of Canada to allow him to run an appropriate electoral campaign.
Let us look at the situation of new Parties. The tax credit is made available on a year-round basis to political Parties that meet certain qualifications. That again is an important political tool. There is status in law which also provides certain privileges. What we are dealing with is a very complex series of rules laid down in the Canada Elections Act, which also includes what we used to call the Canada Election Expenses Act. There are penalties and obligations which have to be lived up to.
The question we have been trying to wrestle with in the ad hoc committee is, what is the judicious balance between allowing anyone who chooses to stand as a candidate and being able to provide the necessary protection for the taxpayer? The question raised by my hon. friend from Mississauga is, how do we deal with a number of parties and candidates so that the elector can make sense of what is going on?
I confess that the committee has spent a great deal of time trying to determine some specific guidelines, and we have come to some general conclusions. These conclusions have been forwarded to the Government, which we hope will bring them down as a legislative package. But the problem is that we were unable to come up with any hard and fast rules.
All of us agree that there could not be a rule which could be interpreted so as to prohibit or inhibit the information of additional political Parties. We could not say that you can only have so many candidates running at a given point in a given riding, because out of the candidates running there may emerge another political Party; an Independent may well be more representative of his constituents than the candidate put forward by the various political Parties. So we did not want to restrict the ability of a constituency to choose whom they
wanted to be their representative. Therefore, we have come to a very delicate situation.
We looked a little bit at raising the $200 limit but came to the conclusion that with the financial advantages that are there, an effective increase would not really be acceptable to Canadians. Even $2,000 in today's economy is not what $200 was in 1882; it is far less in relative value. So it does not make much sense to go about limiting the number of people who can run by raising the $200 fee. By and large, our conclusion was that the $200 was a very modest obstacle. It was an appropriate token to show that one at least was semi-serious and therefore we should not really look any further at it. Instead, what we have done is try to look at other ways of dealing with this phenomenon.
For example, we have tried to make the petition signed by the constituents a much more important part of the process. Right now, as you know, we have to forward a petition signed by 25 people along with the $200. We looked at increasing that number to perhaps 100, 150 or 200. We thought that for serious candidates that would not be a problem. We then came across the problem the Table has had in the last session: how do you justify the petition? How can you tell whether the names on the petition are valid names, particularly in an urban constituency where you may have 200 names from the city but you may have a number of ridings? How do you prove that the 200 names, for example, are actually from the constituency the Member seeks to run in?
We looked at the problem of trying to find another way of proving one's bona fides. We looked at the cost, the petition, we looked at being able to demonstrate that a person was a serious candidate by actually taking the money he is entitled to and spending it. In other words, if one comes into the system and is eligible to have one piece of literature mailed to every household in the projected constituency, then the money is not given to that candidate unless it is actually spent. In other words, they have to come in with the receipt. Right now it is not clear. You have to prove you spent the money, but the process is somewhat open-ended. We have been struggling to close that gap with some administrative rules to make sure that there was proof the money was spent. We did not want people to come in and present ideas and use the money made available through the generosity of the taxpayer in trying to communicate with the taxpayer. I believe we have been able to deal with that particular problem in a relatively acceptable way.
While I have no precise solutions to offer to the problem which I think was legitimately raised by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, the fact that we are getting a large number of spurious candidates, who are recognized as such by the electorate, means that there has to be some way of being able to winnow the candidates down to the serious ones, not the ones who are there for a good time. We have to be able to do that with some delicacy because we do not want accidentally to stomp out a legitimate public movement or those who are running legitimately as Independents to push a particular idea.

We want to make sure the electoral system is available and easy to understand.
It seems to me the way we should approach this problem of electoral reform is to have one principle paramount in our minds. What we are trying to do is not make life better for ourselves; we are trying to make sure that the system reinforces the elector's right to choose whomever he or she wants to represent them. We should not be looking at it as an inconvenience to ourselves to have these people around; we should be looking at it from the point of view of the elector who should have available to him the broadest choice of tools he wants to govern his country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to be able to speak on Bill C-583, which seeks to increase the amount of the deposit which a candidate has to pay to contest an election from $200 to $2,000. I would like to say at the outset that I think it is important for us to realize that under the Canada Elections Act not only is a deposit of $200 required when you run federally, but also there is to be a nomination paper signed by at least 25 electors in the particular district.
Now, to address ourselves to what the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) indicates is the problem, I really question whether it is as great a problem as the Hon. Member seems to think. I know in his particular constituency in the last election there were some seven candidates. I know there were a couple of independents running and I could see where that could present a little bit of a problem. But on the humorous side, I wonder whether he should really squawk too loudly, because the plurality he had in the 1980 election was only about 403 votes and one of the so-called fringe candidates had 405 votes. So I am just wondering whether he should be complaining too loudly about that.
In more serious vein, I would just like to say that there are several issues at stake here. I think some of them really revolve around the whole question of democracy. What are we really doing if we eliminate the opportunity for anyone who wants to run, regardless of political Party?
Every region of the country is not as well loaded, might I say, as the constituency of Mississauga or perhaps some of the central Canada constituencies where $2,000 may not seem to be that much. In rural ridings, some of the western and northern ridings, $2,000 is actually a considerable amount. It could present a bit of a problem to any person who wants to run because not all Parties are funded by various private corporations.

Canada Elections Act
Let us take a look at the return for the thirty-second election. Referring to a couple of constituencies, such as the one of the Hon. Member who presented the Bill, it is very interesting that there were some 46 private corporations which contributed $14,683 toward his election campaign. The Liberals had some 13 private corporations that contributed $2,750 to their campaign; the New Democratic Party did not have any.
Turning to the constituency of Dauphin, my home riding, I notice that the Progressive Conservative Party had 36 private corporations that contributed some $3,930, which obviously was not as substantial as the sum of $14,000 contributed in the Hon. Member's riding.
I raise this issue for Hon. Members of the House because the return of the Chief Electoral Officer is a very thick book and they may not have had occasion to look at it. I think it is worth while because the Hon. Member would not want to discriminate in various parts of Canada. I appreciate the problem in certain parts of urban Canada. But when I look at the whole question of democracy, one of my favourite authors, a past President of the United States, Abraham Lincoln, spoke of democracy as being "the Government of the people, by the people, for the people". Whether it be the Inuit, other aboriginal people or poor people in various parts of the country who make only subsistence livings, I do not feel they should be restricted from running simply because they cannot think of putting down the $2,000 deposit.
It is important to think of the whole question of what we really mean by democracy. Are we trying to bring about disincentives when they are really not necessary? It is really important to think along these lines. Some people may ask whether we have solutions or what exactly we would suggest as an alternative to disincentives. The only oasis of a truly democratic Government is in the Province of Manitoba. Manitoba has had to come to grips with the problem. I refer Hon. Members to the Manitoba Election Act from which the requirement for a deposit has been removed altogether. That is the way it should be.
In fact, I would have been very happy to support the Hon. Member for Mississauga South if he would have decided to remove the deposit altogether. That would have been more in keeping with the whole area of democratic opportunity for any person to run. In Manitoba there is a simple requirement for the nomination papers that 100 or more eligible voters in an electoral division nominate the candidate. That is the way we in Manitoba have dealt with this problem. Therefore, there is opportunity for anyone who is a serious candidate to run. If such a suggestion were made, I am sure some of the problems in Mississauga or other constituencies where there is such a plurality of candidates as seven would be eliminated.
I return to the whole question of a perceived problem in setting up financial barriers for people who may have limited resources. It is important to emphasize this because there is regional disparity in various parts of the country. If one happens to come from a certain area of the country with incomes that range from very modest to some of the highest,

February 16, 1983
Canada Elections Act
then naturally one's perception of the economic means and abilities of those who will be running as candidates will be drastically different from one who comes from a different region of the country. The setting up of two categories of people-those who would be able to run and those who would not be able to run as candidates-is something we would not want to see in the Parliament of Canada.
At one time Abraham Lincoln said:
As I would not be a slave, so I would not be a master. This expresses my idea of democracy.
To paraphrase what Abraham Lincoln was saying in different words, the minute we set up masters and slaves categories we take away the whole notion of democracy in Canada. Even if a person does not have the ability to set aside $2,000 from his ordinary livelihood which is used to provide food, clothing and shelter to run in an election, we feel that he or she may have something to offer the country.
I am reminded of what Harry Emerson Fosdick said when he talked about democracy:
Democracy is based upon the conviction that there are extraordinary possibilities in ordinary people.
1 think this is our conviction, that there are extraordinary possibilities in ordinary people, people who come from various working classes or various ethnic groups in society. We must realize that that type of mix is important in the House of Commons and that we should not have any kind of disincentive to prohibit such people from running for the highest office in the land.
Also it is important to stress what we in the New Democratic Party feel. There should be opportunity for true equality, which implies true equality in terms of the opportunity to run for elected office. Thomas Jefferson said:
The mass of mankind has not been born with saddles on their backs, nor a favoured few booted and spurred, ready to ride them legitimately, by the grace of God.
We do not feel that there should be inequality or that there should be this barrier of $2,000 established so that people who legitimately feel they could run or want to run are not able to do so.
If there is a contest even for nomination, the people who run for it have to expend money for the nomination convention. Such things are not covered. There is an investment of time and other investments which have to be made. I think we would want to uphold this.
This Bill runs counter to the United Nations' Declaration of Human Rights, Article 1, which says the following:
All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
We ought to maintain that right in Canada so that anyone who wants to and is prepared to run for elected office is supported. In this country we ought to maintain the right that anyone who wants to run for elected office who is prepared to and who is supported by other people should have that right. I think there are enough disincentives. The rebate was mentioned. A person must obtain 15 per cent of the votes. If we wanted to eliminate some of the less serious candidates, or
those we perceive to be less serious, then there are opportunities to increase the number of voters who would be placed on a nomination list. That would be one way to deal with that.
We know that in this country there is enough financial inequality. All one has to do is take a look at the way political wheels are greased to see where and to which party the big bucks go.
I think it is important that we do not accept the suggestion made but, rather, that we defeat this Bill and follow the example in Manitoba. In other words, increase the number of eligible nominators. By doing that we would deal with the problem fairly and in a way that does not deprive us of our democracy, yet at the same time dealing with it in a way that addresses the question of equality and fairness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Clause 3 of the Canadian Charter of Rights reads:
Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly and to be qualified for membership therein.
In the explanatory notes in the little red book the Government has published along with the Charter, I find this:
The tradition of democratic rights in Canada is specifically guaranteed by the Charter. Citizens will have a constitutionally enshrined right to vote in elections for Members of the House of Commons or a legislative assembly and to seek election to either of those houses.
There is the standard. Whenever we see a Bill of this sort we must measure the Bill against that standard. We must ask ourselves whether the Bill directly or indirectly hinders the spirit of that Clause. I contend that this Bill very directly takes a run at the right of some citizens to seek public office. As such this Bill should be rejected.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky) who has quoted from a variety of sources to back up that sentiment. I congratulate him for doing so.
1 think this Bill reacts to a perceived inconvenience. Its intent is to erect a barrier to prevent people who somebody somewhere thinks are not serious from running for office. I do not believe that we have the right to decide whether one candidate is a serious candidate and another is not. I believe we should be removing these barriers to people's participation in elections. I do not think we should be raising new ones.
I can sympathize with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I was at an all-candidates meeting in his riding in 1980. About eight or ten of us were there. There were many people who worked for various parties. After the election I took a look at the results both in the Hon. Member's riding and in my riding. We went through this inconvenience of many candidates on the ballot, but after the election the people said it differently than we did. People did not think it was an inconvenience to have numerous candidates.
In the riding of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South 624 people voted for those who could otherwise be designated
February 16, 1983

as not serious. In my riding another 380 people voted for these independent candidates. In our city that meant 1,000 people voted for non-traditional candidates. Who are these nontraditional candidates? There were two Marxist-Leninists, two Libertarians and two Independents. Each one of those candidates had something to say to people in each of our ridings. They had good messages. I did not agree with them, but they had a message they wanted to communicate to the residents of Mississauga, and I think they should be entitled to do that.
Some of those people would see a $2,000 deposit as a genuine barrier against their participation in an election. I do not think we should be putting up that kind of a barrier, certainly not when 1,000 people in my city vote for these candidates.
Even if only one person in my city wanted to vote for one of these candidates, I would still say they are entitled to do that.
Running as a candidate in an election campaign is a viable platform for an ordinary citizen. It is not one that we should be whittling down to a few elite members of the New Democratic Party, the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party. We should be opening up this platform and letting in some of those other ideas.
Anyone who wants to be impressed by this process can take a look American presidential elections. They are perhaps the perfect example. We always look at the two major candidates in American elections, one Democrat and one Republican, but we fail to realize that there are scores of other candidates. We do not hear Americans telling us that these other candidates are an inconvenience or are not serious. But in many respects the Americans are more limited than we are and these people have more rights than our candidates. They have access to TV time, time in public meetings, space in newspapers and so on. The Americans permit this and encourage it. Theirs is a good model for us to follow. These people bring in new ideas and a new perspective into campaigns.
I listened to the concerns of the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). It seems to me that that Member was bringing us practical concerns and mixing up the principle of democratically operated elections with administrative concerns on such matters as excess funds, excess donations and tax credits. Those things are currently handled in law. If the law is inadequate, let us change the law so that the administration of these practical matters is more carefully handled.
We do not need to keep people out of an election campaign just because they give out tax credits or because they collect donations from other Canadians. We govern these concerns now. If the governing of them is inadequate, let us tighten up the administration. As I said, we should not be mixing up the principle of a democratic society and a democratic election with administrative concerns on matters of this nature.
The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River also said that candidates have to prove one's bona fides. I do not know what that means, but that sentiment also ran through the discussion of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South. Somehow there are candidates who have bona fides and candidates who do not have bona fides, or there are candidates who are serious and
Canada Elections Act
others who are not serious. I do not know how you distinguish that. One of my colleagues suggests that citizenship should be the standard. I agree with him. That is the only standard applied in the Charter of Rights and that should be the only standard that we apply. We should not be putting up a barrier in the form of extra deposits or longer lists of nominators or any other administrative device.
We should see that anybody who is serious is taken seriously by the voters. Anybody who is not serious will not be taken seriously by the voters. But let the voters decide. Do not put up a barrier that prevents a candidate's name from going on to the ballot, itself. When the candidate's name is on the ballot, then the true test comes of proving to your fellow citizens that you are serious. Who is going to decide that somebody is a nuisance or is serious? That is where we get into difficulties. We should be looking at the relative advantages and disadvantages that already exist in our system.
The big three Parties begin election campaigns with enormous advantages. They get all the media attention, nationally, locally and regionally. A local candidate can be confident in the knowledge that he has scores and perhaps hundreds of volunteers helping to distribute pamphlets, erect signs, make phone calls and write letters and engage in all those traditional electioneering tactics. Candidates for the big three Parties have all those advantages for making their views known. The small independent candidate who decides to run on his own because he is concerned about something, cannot call upon the national press or hundreds of local volunteers.
There is one exception that I think is a constant reminder to all of us. That exception involves the independent candidate who recently ran in Broadview-Greenwood. I believe he originally ran for the Tory nomination but was then walloped by the Tory establishment and kicked out of the Tory Party. He decided not to stand for that Party and ran as an Independent candidate. He was able to attract national media attention and collect scores of volunteers and approximately twice as many votes as the official Tory candidate in that byelection.
Who would have originally decided whether he was serious or had bona fides? If we had taken the attitude of the Tory Party, that candidate, Mr. Worthington, would have been thrown out and not treated seriously as someone with bona fides.

The Eion. Member says if we want him, we can have him. The Liberal Party is a democratic institution and we would be more than happy to listen to more voices than just those officially sanctioned. We would be quite happy to have him. If he wants to join us, he has to pay his membership fees and prove that he is a member in good standing. That is all he has to do, because we are more than happy to open our doors to the world to attract people, rather than shutting them.
We are not afraid of a man who may have a divergent point of view. We welcome that because we find that it refreshes the Government and our Party. Mr. Worthington can come and talk to us. We were impressed by his character and perseverance. I must say that we were impressed by the fact that he is ready to carry his case right to the people and be so persuasive.
I would not want to discourage any such person who might be interested in joining us. I believe Mr. Worthington said the other day that he would consider becoming a Liberal. If John Turner ever came back to the Liberal Party, then Mr. Worthington would become a Liberal. That is fine; we are anxious to broaden our Party.

speechtext: I would not be that anxious, if I were you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASE IN CANDIDATES' DEPOSIT
speechtext:
I have diverged from my theme which concerns the point raised by both the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). Their point was that a candidate must somehow prove that he or she is serious and has bona fides. I do not believe that that is an appropriate prerequisite. I believe that a candidate must simply put his or her name forward and then let his her fellow citizens decide whether he or she should be a Member of Parliament. That should be the only test. It is not at all appropriate for us to invent new ways to slow those types of candidates down.
In whose view are these people not serious or a nuisance? Who decides this issue? I realize that some can cause problems for those who organize the all-candidate meetings. I know that they can be a nuisance to other local candidates who must wait their turn to answer a question during a meeting since there are so many candidates. I am aware that election organizers find some of these people to be a nuisance. So what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASE IN CANDIDATES' DEPOSIT
speechtext: That is democracy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASE IN CANDIDATES' DEPOSIT
speechtext:
That is right. That is democracy. The Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith), a democrat of the first order, recognizes that principle. He has just articulated it very well.
I must say that it disturbs me when Members start deciding these questions in the House of Commons. It smacks of a great deal of self interest. We should be careful that we are not perceived to be putting up barriers in order to protect our own positions and privileges. We should ensure that these laws welcome newcomers rather than eliminating opportunities for them. I certainly do not believe that we want to be in a position where Canadians feel that we have either protected ourselves or somehow lined our pockets and added to our privileges.
Instead, we should proceed in a way that encourages trust in this institution and in our electoral system. I do not believe a $2,000 nomination barrier will pass the test of trustworthiness.
The Hon. Member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewicky) indicated what the impact of such a barrier would have in lower income areas. Beyond that, even in affluent areas such as the one in which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South lives, it would be seen as an attempt to protect the establishment and keep out newcomers. We cannot afford to give that perception of ourselves. We should be building up confidence that this is a vigorous system that welcomes everyone, including Independent Member like the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) or the candidate who ran in Broadview-Greenwood. We should not put up barriers to their involvement. Nor should we block the public's perception of our openness.
I understand the Hon. Member for Mississauga South. I know why he has raised this question. I was with him in that crowded and excited church gymnasium when Marxist Leninists were saying, "Make the rich pay" and Libertarians were telling everyone to get off the ordinary citizen's back, and when two Independent candidates had ideas that no one could understand. Perhaps they were a nuisance that night. I know that the Member for Mississauga South had a message that he wanted to convey because I did as well. But we had to share our time with these other people. We had to compete for the audience's attention. But we were the better for it. He won his election and I won mine. Obviously, the Independents did not prove their case well enough or we would not be here.
I can understand that he was annoyed by the inconvenience he faced on his path to victory. But those others are entitled to be in his way and propose alternatives in an attempt to trip him up to see if he is good enough to be a Member of Parliament. They have the right to challenge him for that job.
I began by referring to the Charter of Rights. All of us in the House discussed and debated the Charter of Rights. We put into Clause 3 the statement that every citizen of Canada has the right to qualify for membership in the House of Commons. That is in our Charter of Rights, and I do not believe that we want to put forward ideas, seriously or flippantly, that will impede the spirit of that legislation and that great Charter.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASE IN CANDIDATES' DEPOSIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not really anticipated speaking in this debate but the words of the previous speaker so inspired and excited me and raised my interest in this subject that I feel obliged to make a few comments.
On numerous occasions I have been tempted to have a similar opinion as that of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) that it might be advantageous if we did not have a system that lent itself to the existence of frivolous candidates. The first time I ever ran for office during an election was in 1972, and I managed to win that municipal election. However, there were 12 other candidates. I happened
February 16, 1983

to be running against a fellow who was a Nazi leader, and there were a few other very unusual candidates, to say the least. It was very frustrating to attend an all-candidates meeting, having to share time equally with 12 candidates, three-quarters of whom were not in fact what I would consider to be serious candidates.
The temptation is always there to put in place a system which would discourage people from coming forward and running, taking their chances at being elected. The problem, as has already been pointed out by several Hon. Members here today, is that in the final analysis, a truly democratic system is one which somehow strikes a balance between leaving the door open to frivolity and at the same time not making the requirements so stringent that the average Canadian, the ordinary citizen, is unable to run because he simply does not have the money to do it.
As we know, it costs money to run an election these days. We now have in place a system which provides subsidies to candidates who are able to obtain a certain percentage of the vote. However, many candidates are not in fact able to obtain a certain percentage of the vote, and therefore they do not find themselves receiving any public moneys which would be applied toward their campaign. Because of that, they are hard pressed for funds. If, in addition to the demands of their campaign costs, they must also put up a very expensive deposit along the lines which this Private Members' Bill suggests, and I believe it is $2,000, that would indeed work a hardship upon them. I think we would find that many people who would otherwise run, who might otherwise be prepared to participate in the democratic process and take their chances, would in fact be inhibited from taking their chances and putting their names and ideas before the public so that the public can make its judgment. It is a very basic reason as to why I find the Bill, although it is tempting, would not, in the final analysis, be particularly democratic.
What are some of the other considerations which would discourage non-serious candidates from running? I happen to live in an urban area which one can travel around fairly easily because of the short distances involved. However, some ridings in this country are spread out over a very large geographical territory. There are a couple of ridings in the far North, in particular, and one can travel for about 1,500 milles or 2,000 miles and still be in the same riding. We all know how expensive air travel is these days. If a candidate wants to travel around to various parts of the riding and meet all of his would-be constituents, if he has to cover the sort of expenses which would be forced upon him by virtue of the far-flung geography of such very large ridings, and if he must also come up with $2,000 in addition, this would be a very inhibiting factor. It would simply make it impossible for many average Canadians to participate in the democratic process as candidates.
Many ridings have many different towns, and each one of these towns has a newspaper. A candidate might feel obliged
Interest Act
to place an ad in each one of these newspapers. That can be a very expensive endeavour. Just start adding up the costs. 1 remember that several months after an election in which I ran,
I received a bill for $5,000. An enthusiastic supporter of mine had placed many ads in ethnic newspapers on my behalf, but he had not quite bothered to tell me that he had done this, and he had also not paid for them. Suddenly, I received a bill for $5,000 which I was not expecting. My wife was not too happy when 1 told her about it. We managed to sort it out, but it is the sort of expense which can be a tremendous financial burden to a candidate.

that Bill C-471, to amend the Interest Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill was introduced by me for first reading on May 2, 1980, almost three years ago. I want to say right at the outset that I would probably not introduce a Bill in precisely the same wording at the present time. First, let me put on the record what I was attempting to achieve back in May of 1980. If I could simply read from the Bill, which is contained in just one paragraph, it asks that the Interest Act be amended after Section 10 by adding the words, "Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other Act, a mortgagor may, during the term of the mortgage, redeem the mortgage for the amount of principal and interest then due, plus three months further interest".
I will explain the slight difference because of what has happened in the intervening three years, but the objective then, which is similar to my interest today, was to ensure that a person, for reasons not anticipated when the mortgage was signed, would be able, with a suitable penalty, to pay off the mortgage and either refinance the house or move to another house or another type of accommodation. People would have that amount of freedom.
The circumstances today are not essentially changed. Persons sign for five years and sometimes-and my office is concerned with such a case at the present time-there is what is called a three-month cancellation clause in the agreement.

February 16, 1983
Interest Act
However, in the fine print, in the case in question, it states that the three-month cancellation clause cannot come into effect during the first three years of the life of the mortgage. Thus, for good reasons, the occupant of the house is unable to refinance because, obviously, the penalty is the interest for the remaining period.
At that time it seemed to me to be unfair. Sometimes we are accused of trying to protect the consumer too much, but it must be recognized that when a person signs a legal document, there are often many pages of small print, and we cannot expect all persons to be fully aware of all the implications. I therefore thought it would be worth-while to have it written into law so that it would be possible when the circumstances required it, no matter what was written in the contract document, for a person, with a reasonable penalty, to either pay off the mortgage or refinance in many cases, and perhaps even possibly to increase the mortgage.
At that time I had a few pieces of information at my disposal which 1 want to place on the record. I noted, for example, in answers which I received to questions placed on the Order Paper, that the percentage of residential mortgage loans approved by our chartered banks had been increasing steadily through the early seventies. I do not know what the current figure is today, but it is certainly in excess of 30 per cent. I also noticed that amongst persons who owned single, detached dwellings, some 45 per cent had mortgages. I will correct that, Mr. Speaker. Some 53 per cent had a mortgage, of which 7.7 per cent had more than one mortgage. In other words, 47 per cent of single detached dwelling home owners had no mortgage.
Another interesting fact comes from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and I find it rather astonishing. I put the following question:
What is the average delay period per housing unit between the initial default of the owner and the final acquisition by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation of properties that have insured mortgages financed by the chartered banks?
I find the answer, with respect to the last 12 month period, for which it had information, rather surprising. It was as follows:
With respect to claims paid to chartered banks ... the average time lag from the date a borrower defaults on payment until title is conveyed to CMHC under the terms of the mortgage loan insurance policies, is 414 calendar days.
That is approximately 15 months. I find that information rather incredible. Of course, in the meantime the bank is fully protected. It knows that the mortgage is insured and that it is going to be fully paid. In my opinion, the bank, then has no real interest in cleaning up this matter because eventually the amount is going to be paid to it by, of all people, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
What annoys me about this is that while Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation may be a Crown corporation, public funds are involved. I feel we should have some means by which these things could be wound up more quickly. Obviously, if a
person who wants to walk away from a difficult financial situation is unable, because of an agreement, to either refinance or pay off a mortgage through refinancing, then in the final analysis they have little choice but to walk away. It is the taxpayer, the person who put money in Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, who has to pick up the tab.
I feel that every mortgage that is insured by CMHC should have clearly spelled out options in it. I realize-and I know that this is going to be the defence-that only when moneys are lent for a long period at certain fixed interest rates, can the banks also pay high interest rates to those who are willing to lend their money and lock it in for a long period of time.
As a case in point, I happened to note this-quite unconsciously on my part-when I re-arranged my Registered Retirement Savings Plan some five years ago this month. At the time, I thought the best thing to do was to put the money into something at fixed interest rates, and I did so. Of course, within a couple of years the rates started to go up. I inquired then about a penalty in order to put the moneys into some other plan, only to find out, to my chagrin, that the money was locked in. As a matter of fact, those moneys only became free this month, five years after the date I put them into the plan and, of course, the rates have come down again.
The other side of the coin is that last summer when I had some cash available to me I was able to go to the bank when rates were very high and place those moneys at very high interest rates and lock them in for a year. That is a very nice situation and, of course, the banks were only able to give me high interest rates for five years because, in return, they were able to lend the moneys out at a fixed rate over that period of five years to someone else who was perhaps a house owner.
Despite the fact that I have both suffered and benefited from this locked-in feature, in any agreement, whether it be a RRSP or a mortgage, there should be alternatives which allow a person to assess the best way to proceed. Certainly, I feel that it is very unfair in the housing market that any home owner should be locked in for a period of five years with no alternative but to pay the full penalty, in other words, to have to pay the interest for the five year period in order to get out of the mortgage. I feel that is quite unfair. It is something that is often forced upon the poor home owner because he is not able to shop around in the ordinary sense. Very few people go from bank to bank inquiring about rates. They are very much the same no matter which bank you deal with. A lot of this is done on good faith, and when the deal is finally signed with the notary, the people are often not made aware of the full implications.
I have chosen to deal with single, detached dwellings because they serve the argument, and the figures for multidwellings and so on are not substantially different and would only complicate the issue. An answer to a question that I put to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation showed that for single detached dwellings, 38 per cent of mortgages are for $10,000 or less; 37 per cent of mortgages are for mortgages
February 16, 1983

between $10,000 and $20,000; and 17 per cent are for mortgages between $20,000 and $30,000. Those figures are quite interesting, because they indicate that a lot of home owners have mortgages-some 75 per cent-of $20,000 or less. With the present value of housing it is quite apparent that many of those home owners could refinance.
Because of the situation we have found ourselves in within the last year, I would consider it highly desirable, in some circumstances, that the homeowner should be able to refinance without substantial penalty. Take, for example, someone who has become unemployed, and that has happened to too many people in the last short while. If he had, say, a $20,000 mortgage on a house valued between $50,000 and $70,000, and was able to go to the bank and refinance, the extra money might carry him through this difficult period. There are many other reasons why a person might want to refinance a mortgage but if the penalty is the balance of the five years at whatever interest rate he is paying, then obviously he has no choice. Under those circumstances he has to find his moneys from some other source. As everyone is aware, if he goes to a bank he is likely to pay 3 or 4 or 5 points above prime rate, and so will pay a very high interest rate indeed. As well, he has a much shorter repayment term. In other words, in difficult times such as we had last year, I would consider it highly desirable that home owners have easy access to the equity in their homes. If they have built that equity up over the years, they should have access to it through taking out another mortgage. I do not mean a second mortgage because the interest rates on them are too high. I mean access by refinancing.
Earlier I spoke of a case with a three month cancellation clause. I estimated that the penalty would amount to a certain sum and that by adding this penalty to the amount of the principal outstanding and then adding the amount of the moneys necessary for the refinancing of other debts, the total package at current interest rates would result in a monthly payment which was hardly different from the amount presently being paid, but with all the problems of financing for different reasons put into one package. In other words, it would be a lot more convenient.
Because the arrangement to speak on this Bill today was discussed last week, I have not had time to draft the kind of Bill I would like to submit in the new session. It would be worded somewhat differently. 1 recognize that if interest rates for a period of five years are going to be paid to persons who have cash available, obviously those moneys will have to be lent at secured rates for long periods.
Nevertheless, I do not think that we here should be worried about trying to solve the problems of our chartered banks. Let them adjust to the circumstances and let them not do it at the expense of the home owner. While in detail there may be some omissions in this Bill because it is now some three years since I first submitted it, I submit that the intent is clear. I somehow doubt whether this Bill will go into committee for study, but if it should, any difficulties that one might have because of the changed situation today could be looked after by amendments.
Interest Act
The principle remains the same. There should be an option in all mortgages insured by CMHC allowing a home owner to refinance with a reasonable penalty. My suggestion is that that should be three months' interest.

Mr. Speaker, my contribution will not be long. However, there are two or three matters I want to deal with in connection with this Bill. First, all mortgages, certainly those that are insured by Crown corporations, should have an escape clause whereby a person can pay off the mortgage at any time without penalty. I do not understand why a person who has the money should be penalized. If he borrowed $100,000 one or two years earlier and he has paid the interest during that time; if he suddenly has enough money to pay off the mortgage, why should there be a penalty? He is giving back the whole principal plus the interest, which he has already paid. I cannot follow this penalty business. Every mortgage should have an escape clause so that it can be paid off without a penalty.
Second, this Bill may help some people. The Hon. Member mentioned one case. However, it will be used rarely. I have no objection to the Bill, but I wish it had tackled some of the real problems of interest today, those that worry the home owners, farmers and businessmen. There is no end to what could have been put into the Bill.
We recently had a visit from Ontario farmers belonging to the Canadian Farm Survival Group. A farmer and his wife visited my office. They told me the bank had taken over their farm. In fact, the bank was considering whether to allow them to continue living there. Although the bank had sold some of their chattels, it would not give a report on how much it made. It was complete arrogance. When a bank exercises its rights under a chattel mortgage or similar instrument, it should be required by law to show that that money has been applied to the principal and how much.
I was delighted to read of a number of farmers in Ontario who are fed up with the high-handedness of some banks. One man's chattels were being sold. I do not know whether they included cattle, but they did include his machinery, whatever he needed to make a living. The other farmers bid ridiculously low prices, such as $2 or $3 for a tractor, combine or seeder, and then turned it back to the farmer. That is being real neighbourly. I do not see anything wrong with it. They were endeavouring to give that man back the instruments he required.
If the bank takes away the farmer's means of livelihood, how can he possibly pay off his mortgage? The banks are simply confiscating these farms. After a lot of hard work and worry, this man is losing his equity. That is not fair to the farmer.
When I was a teacher in a rural district during the early thirties, I recall an insurance company taking over a farm. One day the youngsters came to school crying because they had been ordered to get out of the house. The insurance company did not care where they went. They simply told them to get out and leave everything the way it was.

February 16, 1983
Interest Act
I looked into that case. In the latter part of the war, the farmer had borrowed money. His wife had tuberculosis. In those days free treatment was not available. Money was not as important as saving his wife's life. Therefore, he borrowed money to take her to doctors for treatment. She could not be cured; she died.
At the time the farmer borrowed the money he thought he would be able to repay it bushel for bushel. When he was kicked off the farm, he had already repaid the debt three times, but still owed as much as he had originally borrowed. Can anyone tell me that is fair? That is completely unfair.
At that time there was a Social Credit Government-I was not a member-headed by the late Premier Eberhart. He established a moratorium so that people would have time to pay their debts. As well, he established the debt adjustment board. In about 1934, federal legislation was introduced by the Bennett Government whereby an independent referee could review loans and payments. If the referee determined that there was good faith on the part of the farmer, the farm was not to be taken away. In fact, under the Alberta legislation, the Creditors' Arrangements Act, it could reduce the sum. Unfortunately, that was a year or two too late for the farmer I have been talking about. After having repaid the debt two and one-half or three times over he was kicked off the farm.
What did the farmer do? He took a granary on skids and moved it to another farmer's property. He could not take any of his equipment. After a lifetime of work, everything was taken from him. He was ruthlessly kicked off his farm. The insurance company had the gall to threaten him with a lawsuit if he did not take the granary back. They were vicious about it. Thank goodness legislation was introduced after that which saved others from a similar situation. Scores of farmers with viable farm operations in Alberta would have lost their farms had the legislation not been introduced at that time. The Farmers' Creditors' Arrangement Act and the debt adjustment legislation in the Province of Alberta and the moratorium saved their farms and they were able to get a proper settlement. In some cases it was reduced, and there were some cases where the farmer had not played the game, and the Debt Adjustment Board knew what to do with these farmers also. But most of them had played the game in economic conditions over which they had no control. When you have a system which is going to make you pay your debt two and three times over and still owe as much as you borrow, how can any ordinary person overcome that?
I would like to say to the Hon. Member that I wish something like that had been put in the Bankruptcy Act which we have before us. It is useless to anyone who is in difficulty today. We need the Farmers' Creditors' Arrangement Bill, or something to that effect, attached to it so that it would have some teeth in it, some way of settling these matters in a fair and equitable way. These are the things which are worrying me. Farmers are being kicked off their farms and losing their entire equity.
We may think it is a joke and say that the farmers brought it on themselves. Well, the farmers in many, many cases did not bring it on themselves. It was brought about by economic conditions over which they have no control. For instance, the sudden rise of interest rates a short time ago completely changed the picture. People who had bought homes and had to renew the mortgage at a rate which was way beyond their wages, the farmer whose farm cost him far beyond the produce which he could sell, the picture was changed for them. The banks did not play very fair, either. A farmer from Ontario, well educated in agriculture, expanded his operations just before the interest rates started to climb. He wanted to have something for his family, and he bought an old farm. And then the interest rates went up. The banker had said to him when he mortgaged the property. "Don't worry, we'll see you through on this. We'll give you time if there is a rise in interest rates. We'll play fair with you." The bank manager was then moved away and the new bank manager had no heart at all, no interest except in getting that land or getting that money, without any fairness at all attached to it.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, we had some legislation to protect these people. They need protection. That is what we should be doing in this country, protecting our farmers who have equity in the land who are playing the game. We need to have our homes protected so we are not kicked out on the street so that the money lenders can receive their full supply of money. Certainly, we want to be fair to those who are caught in the trap. Let us not give all our sympathies to the people who have all the money and forget about those having tough times because of conditions which they had no part in bringing about.
1 wish, Mr. Speaker, we could have some changes like that, then I could get enthusiastic about this Bill. I cannot now get enthusiastic about it. I suppose the Government will talk it out anyway innocuous as it is. However, 1 am not going to worry about that on this Bill. I will worry about it with some other Bills. But if this Bill had some teeth in it to help those having a tough time meeting their payments, then I would be very, very concerned.

Mr. Speaker, it is always stimulating to listen to the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) who, this afternoon, was retreating, and I welcome this retreat, into the views which he must have held in his earlier days as a Social Creditor in Alberta. I am always pleased to listen to the Hon. Member for Bow River go after the banks, because the more he talks, the more he sounds like one of that great socialist horde upon which he heaps so much abuse in so many of his other speeches in the House. Unfortunately, we do not have full opportunity to go into it, but I wonder how the Hon. Member for Bow River fits his view of the banks into his general philosophy of free enterprise and into the general conspiracy theory about world socialism, which so many of his colleagues subscribe to. It would be interesting if at some time the Hon. Member would expand on that for us.
