I was certainly moved by the sympathy which the Hon. Member displayed for farmers who are the victims of certain economic circumstances beyond their control. What is unfortunate is that the Hon. Member, and many others of the political tradition which he represents, have not been able to muster the same sympathy for workers who are the victims of economic circumstances which are beyond their control. When seen through the Conservative mind, there is something noble about farmers rebelling against economic circumstances which have been imposed upon them. I agree. I believe it is noble and 1 believe it is called for, but yet through the minds of the farmers, there seems to be something ignoble about workers rebelling against the economic circumstances which have been imposed upon them from beyond, whether it be from the metropolis to the hinterland, whether it is the banks moving in on them, or whatever the circumstances might be.
I believe this is one of the unfortunate divisions within the country, that so often a distinction has been made between the economic problems of the agricultural community and the economic problems of workers in industry in our cities. This is the gap which the political tradition, out of which 1 consider myself to come, tried to bridge, and, indeed, did bridge in many respects in 1933 through a coalition of farmers and workers and, of course others, in the formation of the CCF. That Party wanted to overcome the false distinction between the problems which farmers faced as a result of economic decisions made from afar, and the problems that workers faced as a result of economic decisions made from afar. 1 just wanted to say to the Hon. Member for Bow River.
I, like others, support the principle of the Bill. Certainly, people should have more opportunity to get out of mortgages which they signed at a time of high interest rates, now that interest rates have gone down. It seems to me to be absolutely criminal, Mr. Speaker, that these people are in the position in which they are, that all their disposable income, and indeed in some cases more income than they actually have, has to go toward paying interest, and they end up after the period of time is over having paid only a very minimal sum on the principal. I, myself, had the good fortune in 1978 to sign a five-year mortgage. I am only paying, I believe, 1014 per cent or 1016 per cent, and am amazed at how little I have paid on the principal in the last four and a half years.
This is something, Mr. Speaker, which I believe is at the root of the problems in our economic system, that people must pay out so much for so little. I believe it is a sign of a complete breakdown of economic morality in this country. And 1 would like to remind the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and the Hon. Member for Bow River that the New Democratic Party moved amendments to the Bank Act in the summer of 1980 which would have had the effect of doing what both these Hon. Members have stood up in this House and said they support. But we did not receive the support of those Hon. Members at that time. Indeed, if you will recall that debate, the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party together voted many, many times against NDP amendments, one of which would have had the effect of outlawing penalties on prepayment of loans and preventing the banks from calculating
Interest Act
interest in such a way as to assure them of a windfall in the event of early payment.
These are the kinds of things we tried to bring in at the time we were reconsidering the Bank Act. And that is not something we get to do very often. The Bank Act only comes up for amendment once every ten years if we are lucky, and my Liberal and Conservative colleagues blew it at that time. They co-operated to vote against our amendments, I wanted to bring that to the attention of the House and all those who are interested in this issue. Whether the Hon. Member for Bow River likes it or not, when it comes to the Bank Act and banking in this country, the Liberals and the Conservatives are of one mind. They demonstrated this on some 20 to 30 votes at that time, if my memory serves me correctly. That is something to keep in mind.
While we are talking about high interest rates, another thing to keep in mind is that the Liberals and the Conservatives, if what I am told is correct and I believe it to be correct, again co-operated back in 1966 when we saw the beginning of this problem. The Liberals and Conservatives allowed themselves to be fooled by the argument that if they took off the 6 per cent limit, the competitive market place, which Members to my right are always foaming at the mouth about, would provide lower interest rates. The banks would be competing with each other in the money markets, interest rates would go down, and what a wonderful thing this new deregulation of interest rates would be. What a wonderful economic gift to the Canadian people it would be. Well, we all know what happened, Mr. Speaker. You can hardly say the control which a small number of banks in this country exercise over the economy is a sort of laboratory of free enterprise.
So what happened, Mr. Speaker? Interest rates climbed and climbed and climbed. At that time we opposed the fundamental and far reaching change in credit policy which I am referring to. At the request of the chartered banks which were seeking to break into the mortgage lending, consumer loans and credit card business, usury laws were abolished. I think that was a big mistake, not just economically but also conceptually. I tend to have perhaps an old-fashioned view of this. I take the view that the notion of usury should have been maintained and that we have gone too far down the road toward morally neutralizing various things like interest rates.
The Small Loans Act was there until 1980.

So in 1966, for the first time in Canadian history, there was no statutory limit on the rate of interest which could be charged on bank loans. Now, we said at that time that a more sensitive and socially responsible alternative would have been, if you are going to do that, to impose limits on all lending institutions rather than eliminating them completely. But we were not listened to. There have been many occasions over the years when we have not been listened to in the House, when we predicted something was going to happen

if you did this, and everybody said: You are wrong. But we turned out to be right. This is one of the many cases where we have turned out to be right. No one can get up and deny that since 1966 interest rates have risen dramatically. The cost of money has risen dramatically. The kind of competition envisaged at that time did not materialize and the Canadian people have not benefited from that change.
You voted to repeal the Small Loans Act in 1980, which took interest rate ceilings off credit unions.

Mr. Speaker, that is one of the reasons I did not bother to answer the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), because he was not in his seat. But he does refer to what was done in 1980 with regard to the Small Loans Act, and I know the reason why and he knows the reason why. It is because the credit unions were being hurt by high interest rates. I make no apologies for our support for that change. It does not take away from the substance of my argument in the least.
What we need to do at this time, Mr. Speaker, is to look behind the problem of whether or not people can get out of these mortgages, to the whole financial system in this country and the need for more regulation of the banks in the public interest. That is the kind of direction in which we tried to move this Parliament in the summer of 1980. We believed then that the Act as it was proposed did nothing to protect consumers and small businessmen. It enhanced corporate concentration. It was an Act written to benefit the banks, not the people of Canada. We suggested some amendments, and I would just like to go over them for the record before I sit down so the Government can have the pleasure of talking out this Bill.
We suggested that the Minister of Finance be given the responsibility to monitor the fairness of all interest rates and charges and roll back any unjustifiable increases and charges of any kind by a bank, including credit cards. We opposed the introduction of foreign banks into Canada. We wanted complete information on the cost of loans to consumers and any other bank customers. We wanted to outlaw, as I said before, any penalties on prepayment of loans and prevent the banks from calculating interest in such a way as to ensure them a windfall in the event of an early payment. We wanted to provide for a complete code of financial disclosure and accountability by the banks. We wanted to stop the banks from taking over certain areas of small business such as car leasing and computer data processing. We wanted to give protection to many farmers and cattlemen in the event of a customer being unable to pay for produce. Finally, we said, either we make the banks accountable to the public or we give them a blank cheque to control large sections of the economy. That blank cheque is exactly what Liberal and Conservative Members who spoke today, and their respective caucuses signed in the summer of 1980 when they co-operated against
the NDP to pass that Bank Act without the NDP amendments offered at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record that those amendments to the Bank Act regarding the protection of produce in transit where the purchaser has been taken over by the bank were proposed and passed by the Government, and it was Government Members, along with other Members of the committee, who turned back the banks from getting involved in consumer leasing. I must say, though, that I am quite disappointed after hearing these remarks from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) that his Party did not see fit to have someone attend the meetings which are held during the month of September in the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. We heard witnesses from across Canada, and a lot of these ideas were discussed at that time.
However, I want to get back to the Private Members' Bill we are discussing here tonight. I want to commend the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) on bringing forward his proposal. I do not believe, however, he goes far enough. I fully realize that there are two sides to such an issue and that two parties have to get together to sign an agreement or to sign a mortgage-the borrower and the lender. Just yesterday 1 received a letter from a businessman in my area who took out a $200,000 mortgage a couple of years ago at 18.25 per cent interest. Now he has found funds at a lower interest rate and the lender wants a $20,000 prepayment penalty to pay off the mortgage. He cannot possibly raise that amount of money at the present time. Therefore, he is faced with either going into receivership or trying to sell off some of his assets to pay the prepayment penalty in order to remortgage at a lower rate.
I can well understand the frustration which faces someone like this, but I believe that there is a responsibility on both sides. Rather than having a maximum three-month penalty on prepayment, perhaps there should be something related to the interest rate on the Small Business Bond. Perhaps the banks could accept a three-month penalty at half the bank prime rate plus 2 per cent, which would cut the penalty being asked of this particular gentleman to about $4,500 instead of $20,000. We must realize that when the particular trust company made the mortgage, it was investing someone's fund. In turn, it was committed to a five-year term certificate or some certificate tied to a fixed interest rate. Consequently, it could not very well get off the hook without some form of compensation. I believe that both sides should contribute and suffer the loss.
I would like to go further than just this particular area. I believe we have to re-examine what is happening in the business sector, particularly in the small business and agricultural sectors about which we have heard so much in the last few days. I should like to refer to the series of meetings which took place in September when the Canadian Chamber of Commerce appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. It made a proposal that if we were to look at the adjustments to the capital gains tax
February 16, 1983

structure as such, perhaps we should look at the length of tenure or ownership and relate taxes on that basis. This would catch the windfall speculator and give a break to those people who have invested their lifetime savings back into a particular business or farm. That is one alternative which I believe is very practical and workable.
The other alternative is to apply indexation to capital gains tax. At the present time farm values have decreased between 25 per cent and 30 per cent over the last year or year and a half. Perhaps it is an opportune time to take a look at the possibility of applying indexation to capital gains tax so that we are not taxing away a person's retirement fund but are keeping pace with inflation and protecting the investment for which he worked so hard over the years and which he put back into his operation.
Another area at which we should take a look in these difficult times was mentioned before in the House-the fact that Canadians are regarded as great savers. In 1981 they salted away something like $17 billion worth of personal savings. It is required in today's economy; it is required for small-businessmen and farmers. We should take a look at what could be done with that money if we ensured that it was well secured for the investor. Normally when a businessman or farmer sells, he tries to reinvest the funds in guaranteed term certificates or something that he knows will give him security in his retirement years and allow him the freedom and type of pleasures which perhaps he did not enjoy during his lifetime of labour.
In this particular area we should look at the possibility of investment incentives to private individuals investing in fixed capital assets. There is no reason that a businessman who sells out to his son could not take back a mortgage. I remember that was the way it was when I started farming. A private individual gave me a mortgage, and if I could not make a payment on principal the first year, he was lenient and said, "You will have a better year next year; give me the money when you can". We did this, but in those days we did not have the huge investments of today, although we had tough times.
We should look at the private investor and bear in mind that when a businessman goes to the bank for a small-business loan, or a farmer goes for a farm improvement loan, it is Government guaranteed. We should do the same for private investors on fixed capital assets. For example, if a son wanted to take over a farm from his father, the father could take back a mortgage and know that his investment was secure. I realize that there would have to be some mechanism to protect the public interest and to ensure that the Government was not loaded up with a bunch of bad debts. We have that mechanism in the field at the present time. We have it through the CASE workers in the Federal Business Development Bank. They are experienced businessmen, most of them retired, and they know a good investment when they see it. Also, we have that mechanism through Farm Credit Corporation supervisors. This is a vehicle through which we could enhance the investment climate for the small investor who would like to assist a son, a
Interest Act
daughter or another member of the family to become established in business. This is only one additional step at which we could look. We could go even further. For example, if they are willing to take back mortgages at interest rates lower than the prevailing rate, we should also look at the possibility of giving them a break on income tax payable on interest earned.
We should bear in mind that we are doing this for the banks through the Small Business Bond. They are paying half the bank prime rate plus 2 per cent or 3 per cent. Why should it not be available to the private investor, if it would help a young person to get started with his farm or small business? I believe such an opportunity would bring out a lot of that investment capital which we sorely need in today's economy.
These are the areas at which we have to look, in addition to the proposal of the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil. I wish to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for his comments on the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and the amendments incorporated in Bill C-653. I tried to incorporate a prepayment penalty ceiling which I believed was fair and reasonable to both borrowers and lenders.
Consequently, as we look at these various measures, I think mechanisms can be put in place to help those in need, particularly those in the small-business, farming and fisheries sectors. In way of a brief recap, I am talking about readjusting the prepayment penalties to a more reasonable level; changes in the capital gains tax structure, either those suggested by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce or through indexation; investment incentives to private investors, small businesses and agricultural operations on fixed capital assets; and assisting young people to become established in businesses of their choice.
These measures alone are not sufficient. We have come through a severe period of high interest rates, low commodity prices, and a recession which has gripped most countries of the western world. In view of the fact that commodity prices are very low at the present time, these measures alone, which we have discussed so far, will not solve the problem and give the long-term security required in this sector. Look at the opportunities available to us. Other countries view Canada as a stable nation, a nation to be trusted which is not one of the super powers. There is a feeling in other parts of the world of wanting to deal with Canada. Many nations do not want to become obligated to one of the super powers.
In this context, I want to point to the various farm organizations and the type of security they enjoy when the economy is booming. It reflects back to other sectors of the small business world, to the allied industries that supply their equipment and other needs of the farming sector. If we are going to bring that type of stability into this area, then we need to have other mechanisms in place. I am referring here to a piece of legislation that is before the House at the present time a waiting report stage and third reading. Bill C-85 will provide a mechanism that has been asked for by the farm organizations of

We know why you are here, Mr. Speaker. I wonder why there are so many of them over there.
This is a very serious matter. This is the tenth time that I have introduced the House a measure that would have the effect of removing every semblance of the appearance of conflict of interest in the broad question of accident investigation in this country. In the western world Canada remains one of the few countries which has not long ago taken the prudent step of separating from those agencies responsible for the

February 16, 1983

promulgation of regulations the responsibility for investigating accidents that occur within the ambit of these very regulations.
We have seen conflict. We have felt the consequences of that conflict. Yesterday in St. John's, Newfoundland, a memorial service was held for the men who lost their lives on the Ocean Ranger. Let me suggest at the outset that had the concept of my Bill, currently Bill C-337, been accepted by Government when it was introduced some ten years ago, the conflict that exists today would never have occurred. There would have been jurisprudence. There would have been a basis from which to proceed with a legally constituted inquiry. We all know what the difficulties are.
Let me review the situation for a moment so that Hon. Members over there will be aware. Going back to the days when the present Speaker of the other place was Minister of Transport, he agreed in principle to the establishment of a multi-model, independent, impartial commission of investigation. In those days we linked it as well to the principles of an impartial safety board. Without going into the events in great detail, I will put this on the record. I suggest Members read the debates surrounding Bill C-66. As well, there were Bills C-85, C-33, C-226, C-109, C-344, C-40, C-473 and presently Bill C-337. We are given to understand that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) will shortly bring before the House his own version that will apply to aviation accidents. If we are to believe that the Government followed the recommendations of Justice Dubin's Report, the Board to be established will ensure impartiality with respect to safety and particularly with respect to investigation. That Board will report to this Chamber through a Minister other than the Minister of Transport. Therefore, since I have no reason to believe otherwise, I trust that the Minister's piece of legislation will, in fact, be impartial.
If Members read Justice Dubin's first volume, which was written as a result of the findings of the Commission that was established by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) when he was Minister of Transport three years ago, and compare it with the subject matter of Bill C-337, they will find them to be essentially identical. In other words, it involves the commonsense principle, which was agreed to by a succession of Ministers of Transport, starting with the Hon. Jean Marchand, now Speaker of the Senate, up to and including the present Minister of Transport, that what is good for air safety is good for the marine mode, the surface mode, pipelines and every form of transportation in this country that falls within the ambit of federal regulations.
It is shortsighted to establish a board that deals with only one mode of transportation. It is a waste of time of the House. Beyond that, it constitutes a further delay in ridding the image of conflict of interest in Canada. When we see the legislation we will know how the Government will pursue evidence from across the border relating to that. We will understand quite clearly what the Government is doing. It began this procedure in 1968. We are now in 1983. Why do we have this delay?
Transport Accidents
Why do we permit ourselves to be viewed with mistrust and suspicion by countries like Britain, United States, Australia, West Germany, Japan, New Zealand and Norway because of the conflict that we continue to permit to surround the investigation of transportaiton accidents in our country?
My Bill is straightforward and seizes itself with the necessity of eliminating that conflict. It comes as a result of an expressed concern throughout the transportation industry in Canada, including aviation, marine, rail, interprovincial pipelines and interprovincial trucking. It flowed from a concern expressed by those interested communities that this Parliament should take some time to review the situation and produce legislation which would eliminate that appearance of conflict of interest.
We have not seen that legislation. As I said, we would not even have had Justice Dubin's recommendations had it not been for the distinguished Member for Vegreville during his tenure as Minister of Transport. When we did get Justice Dubin's Report all that we saw done was the setting up of an ad hoc committee to study it. I would remind Hon. Members that one of the people named to that committee was the then Air Administrator, Mr. Walter McCleish, who in fact was the very subject of an extraordinary amount of criticism by Mr. Justice Dubin in his first and second volumes.

speechtext: Sit down, blabbermouth.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: FEDERAL TRANSPORT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY ACT
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has the floor. Our standing orders provide that when a Member has been recognized to make a speech, he should not be interrupted. The Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East.

subtopic: FEDERAL TRANSPORT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL TRANSPORT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not one of them over there can stand up in the Chamber and point to one single thing that they have ever done. I have been promoting a good idea for 12 years. Do you want to know why it has been rejected over those years? Do you want to know why it continues to be rejected today? It is because it is a good idea and makes common sense. It will help the transportation industry and help the public image of Canada. It was rejected because it came from the Conservative side of the House. We thought of it first, so they do not want to implement it.
Simply because those Members appear to be interested at last, perhaps I will move a motion. Pursuant to Standing Order
8(4)(a) I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby):
That the House continue to sit beyond the ordinary hour of adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of Bill C-337, an Act to provide for the constitution of a Federal Transport Commission of Inquiry, on the second reading stage.
I commend that motion to Members of the House. Let us see them put their money where their mouth is.

subtopic: FEDERAL TRANSPORT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY ACT
speechtext: Sit down, blabblermouth.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: FEDERAL TRANSPORT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY ACT

And more than 25 Members having risen:

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: FEDERAL TRANSPORT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY ACT
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 8(4)(b), the motion is deemed to have been negatived.
